summary: A misconception-correction session on the difference between mass and weight, working toward calculating weight on the Moon.
student_turns: I don't get why my teacher said my mass and weight aren't the same thing, I thought they were basically the same?
But if I stand on the bathroom scales, isn't that just telling me my mass in kg?
So if weight's actually a force, does that mean it should be in newtons instead of kilograms?
Okay so would my weight be different if I went to the Moon, even though my mass stays exactly the same?
How would I actually work out what my weight would be on the Moon, is there an equation for that?

summary: A discouraged student anxious about the maths in physics, working through rearranging the specific heat capacity equation.
student_turns: I'm honestly rubbish at the maths bit in physics, I understand the theory but the equations just stress me out.
This question wants me to work out the specific heat capacity and I don't even know where to start.
I know the equation's change in thermal energy equals mass times specific heat capacity times temperature change, but I don't know how to rearrange it to get specific heat capacity on its own.
I always mess it up when I try to rearrange equations, is there some kind of trick or do I literally just have to memorise how to move each one around?
Can we try one together with actual numbers so I can check if I've actually got it this time?

summary: An exam-prep session on recalling the density equation and keeping its units straight for the required-practical questions.
student_turns: My exam's coming up in a few weeks and I still don't know all the equations we're meant to have memorised, not the ones on the sheet.
Can you test me on a few instead of me just reading the list over and over, that never actually sticks for me.
Is density mass divided by volume, or volume divided by mass, I always get it the wrong way round.
And what units go with density, because I've seen kg per metre cubed in some questions and grams per centimetre cubed in others.
What's a good way to remember the units for something like density so I don't mix them up under exam pressure?
